title: Weight-Space Audit of MIT-p50c and DNA Weight Editing (SGNE-CC) on Qwen3.5-0.8B at a 32,768-Token Generation Limit (EN / RU)
authors: unclear (no author name in text; GitHub account Nondual-Observer)
editor_models: unclear (SGNE-CC search procedure not released; MIT-p50c is the MIT WSP edit)
domain: math reasoning, symbolic logic, code generation, multilingual text generation

headline_result.text: Under greedy decoding the MIT-p50c edit solved only 4 of 100 MATH-500 problems versus 44 for the norm-preserving SGNE-CC patch, while under model-card sampling on the full 500 problems MIT-p50c solved 51.8% and SGNE-CC 47.0%.
headline_result.quote: Under strict grading, Base solves none of the 100 problems, MIT-p50c solves 4, and SGNE-CC solves 44: the paired difference is +41/−1 problems (exact paired McNemar test, p = 1.96 × 10⁻¹¹).

key_claims.claim: The MIT-p50c edit is nearly rank-one in both edited layers and more than doubles some column norms, while SGNE-CC rotates columns and keeps norms within about 0.16%.
key_claims.quote: the first singular mode accounts for over 99.999% of update energy. Individual column norms increase by up to 114.3%, reaching more than twice their pretrained length.

key_claims.claim: The MIT-p50c gain depends strongly on decoding settings: on the same 100 problems it went from 4 correct under greedy decoding to 45 under model-card sampling with presence penalty.
key_claims.quote: switching to model-card settings changes MIT-p50c's score in the direct PyTorch run from 4 to 45 of 100 (+42/−1, p = 1.00 × 10⁻¹¹).

key_claims.claim: In a direct PyTorch run on all 500 MATH-500 problems under model-card settings, base, MIT-p50c and SGNE-CC solved 7.8%, 51.8% and 47.0%, with SGNE-CC four times shorter.
key_claims.quote: Base solves 39 problems (7.8%), MIT-p50c solves 259 (51.8%), and SGNE-CC solves 235 (47.0%; McNemar +56/−80, nominal p = 0.048).

key_claims.claim: Both edits, selected only on math, transfer to logic and code: on BBH-160 base solved 3, MIT-p50c 81 and SGNE-CC 66 of 160.
key_claims.quote: Base solves 3 of 160 problems (1.9%), MIT-p50c solves 81 (50.6%), and SGNE-CC solves 66 (41.3%).

key_claims.claim: SGNE-CC is significantly worse than MIT-p50c on multilingual word problems even after a clustered test.
key_claims.quote: On MGSM-240, SGNE-CC solves 100 of 240 language instances (41.7%) versus 137 (57.1%) for MIT-p50c and 62 (25.8%) for Base.

key_claims.claim: Shorter, formally finished output does not guarantee faithful content.
key_claims.quote: This case shows that formal completion guarantees neither instruction fidelity nor preservation of prompt facts.

limitations_stated.text: One run per prompt; seed variance is unmeasured.
limitations_stated.quote: All direct PyTorch runs record one output per prompt (seed 0), so seed-to-seed variance inside the PyTorch generator is unmeasured

limitations_stated.text: The search procedure that produced SGNE-CC is not released.
limitations_stated.quote: The rotation-angle search procedure is not released

limitations_stated.text: The two edits differ in several factors at once, so the causal role of norm preservation is not isolated.
limitations_stated.quote: the empirical results below are consistent with this hypothesis, yet do not isolate the causal effect of norm preservation on their own.

notes_for_review: An independent audit of the MIT Qwen3.5-0.8B MATH-500 edit: it recomputes the edit geometry and shows that the MIT gain largely disappears under greedy decoding without the presence penalty (4/100), which is direct evidence that the reported gain is tied to the sampling setting. Under model-card settings the MIT number is roughly reproduced (51.8% in PyTorch vs 48.1% reported). The competing SGNE-CC patch is released but how it was found is not, and it may or may not involve an LLM. Single seed, no multiplicity correction, no fine-tuning baseline; author identity is not given in the text.
